newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UN Council retains sanctions against Libya.
newsitem.headline: UN Council retains sanctions against Libya.

text.p: The Security Council on Thursday retained sanctions against Libya despite pleas for a compromise by Arab and African groups on where suspects of the 1988 Lockerbie bombing should stand trial, its president said.
The council's decision followed a periodic 120-day review of the sanctions, which include an air embargo, a ban on arms sales and the downgrading of diplomat relations.
They also include a freeze on some Libyan assets abroad and a ban on certain types of equipment used in oil terminals and refineries. But they do not affect oil exports or oil drilling equipment.

Both the Arab League and the Organization of African Unity in a June 27 letter argued that the trial of the two Lockerbie suspects should not be held in Scotland or the United States but in a neutral country. Alternatively, they could be tried by Scottish judges under Scottish law at the seat of the World Court in The Hague. Their case was argued Thursday in the council mainly by Egypt, Kenya and Guinea-Bissau.

The council's decision, announced by Council President Peter Osvald of Sweden, followed a letter from the United States, France and Britain accusing both organizations of attempting to "misrepresent" the controversy as a dispute between Libya and their countries.
"We do not believe that council decisions should be a matter of negotiation; they should be obeyed in full," the letter said.

The sanctions were first enacted in 1992 because of Libya's failure to extradite to Britain or the United States two alleged intelligence officers indicted in both countries on charges of planting a bomb aboard Pan Am flight 103, which exploded over the Scottish village of Lockerbie killing 270 people, including 11 on the ground.
The sanctions also penalized Libya for not cooperating in the investigation into the 1989 bombing of a French UTA airliner over Niger which killed all 171 people aboard.
